Honest order: split first, then fit the selector (or scaler) and the model on the training folds only, and apply them unchanged to the validation fold.
A scikit-learn Pipeline enforces the honest order automatically: every step inside it is refit within each training fold.

blocks.md: Leakage also hides in how rows relate. **Group leakage**: several rows come from the same patient, user or device; if the same patient lands in both training and validation, the model can recognize the person instead of learning the disease. Split by group (scikit-learn `GroupKFold` keeps each group on one side). **Time leakage**: on time series, a random split trains on the future to predict the past. Split by time so that validation always comes after training (`TimeSeriesSplit`).

Lesson 6 rested on the **i.i.d. assumption**: training and future data come from the same distribution. Deployment often breaks it, which is called **distribution shift**. Under **covariate shift** the inputs change but the rule linking them to labels does not, for example a classifier trained on photos and then shown cartoons. Under **label shift** the class frequencies change while each class still looks the same, for example a diagnosis model trained before a disease became more common (Dive into Deep Learning, section 4.7). No validation split from the old data can reveal either; monitor live inputs and outcomes.

Finally, always compare with a **baseline** that needs no learning: predict the training mean for regression, or the most frequent class for classification (scikit-learn's `DummyClassifier`, documented under [dummy estimators](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html#dummy-estimators)). On the fraud data of lesson 10 that baseline scores 99 percent accuracy. A model that cannot clearly beat it has learned nothing useful, however good its number looks.

Suspiciously good validation results are a bug report until proven otherwise. Check that every preprocessing step was fit on training rows only, that no group or time period straddles the split, and that no feature is recorded after the outcome it predicts.

Fit everything (scalers, feature selection, imputation) inside the training fold, ideally with a Pipeline. Split by group or by time when rows are related. Expect distribution shift in deployment, and always report a trivial baseline next to your model.

blocks.question: A team predicts hospital readmission. Each patient has several visits, and they split the visits randomly into train and validation. Validation AUC is 0.95; on new patients it is 0.70. What is the most likely cause?
options: Visits from the same patient appear on both sides of the split, so validation rewards recognizing patients
The learning rate was too high
AUC is the wrong metric for readmission
The model is underfitting
blocks.explain: This is group leakage: patient-specific details let the model match validation visits to training visits of the same person. Splitting by patient (GroupKFold) would have shown the 0.70 before deployment.

blocks.question: A spam filter trained last year sees a new wave of spam that uses image attachments instead of text. The meaning of 'spam' has not changed. What kind of problem is this?
options: Label shift
Covariate shift: the input distribution moved
Group leakage
Overfitting to the training set
blocks.explain: The inputs (what spam looks like) changed while the rule from content to label did not: covariate shift. Label shift would be the share of spam changing while each class still looks the same.

blocks.question: Before splitting, you fill missing values in a column with the mean of the whole dataset. Is that leakage?
options: No, means are harmless
Only if the column is the label
Yes: the fill value used held-out rows; compute it on the training fold only
Only for time series
blocks.explain: Imputation is a fitted preprocessing step like scaling. Its fill value should be learned from training rows and reused for validation and test. The effect is usually small for a mean, but the habit matters, and a Pipeline makes it automatic.

lessons.title: Build it: a complete training loop in NumPy

blocks.md: Time to put every piece together in about 40 lines of NumPy: synthetic data, a train/validation/test split, standardization fit on the training rows, logistic regression trained by minibatch SGD with an L2 penalty, early stopping on validation loss, and one final evaluation on the test set with precision and recall. Each line maps to a lesson of this course.

The data: 600 points in two classes, each a cloud of two features. The second feature is measured on a scale 40 times larger than the first, on purpose, so that scaling matters. The split is 60/20/20: 360 training, 120 validation and 120 test rows.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
n = 600                                   # two overlapping clouds
y = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
X = rng.normal(size=(n, 2)) * [1.0, 40.0] + np.c_[y*1.5, y*60.0]
idx = rng.permutation(n)                  # split 60 / 20 / 20
tr, va, te = idx[:360], idx[360:480], idx[480:]
mu, sd = X[tr].mean(0), X[tr].std(0)      # statistics from TRAIN only
Z = (X - mu) / sd

def loss(w, b, i, lam=0.0):
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(Z[i] @ w + b)))
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12)
    ce = -np.mean(y[i]*np.log(p) + (1-y[i])*np.log(1-p))
    return ce + lam * w @ w
blocks.caption: Part 1: data, split, standardization with training statistics only (lessons 3 and 11), and the cross-entropy loss with an optional L2 term (lessons 1 and 8). np.clip avoids taking the log of exactly 0.

blocks.code:
w, b = np.zeros(2), 0.0
lr, lam, B, patience = 0.1, 1e-3, 32, 5
best, wait = np.inf, 0
for epoch in range(200):
    order = rng.permutation(tr)           # reshuffle every epoch
    for k in range(0, len(order), B):
        i = order[k:k+B]
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(Z[i] @ w + b)))
        g = p - y[i]                      # (p - y) per example
        w -= lr * (Z[i].T @ g / len(i) + 2*lam*w)
        b -= lr * g.mean()
    v = loss(w, b, va)
    if epoch % 5 == 0:
        print(epoch, round(loss(w, b, tr), 4), round(v, 4))
    if v < best - 1e-4:
        best, wait, keep = v, 0, (w.copy(), b)
    else:
        wait += 1
        if wait == patience: break
w, b = keep                               # restore best validation weights
pred = (Z[te] @ w + b) > 0                # threshold p = 0.5
tp = np.sum(pred & (y[te] == 1)); fp = np.sum(pred & (y[te] == 0))
fn = np.sum(~pred & (y[te] == 1))
print("stopped at epoch", epoch, "w", w.round(3), "b", round(b, 3))
print("test precision", round(tp/(tp+fp), 3), "recall", round(tp/(tp+fn), 3))
blocks.caption: Part 2: minibatch SGD with reshuffling (lesson 4), the (p - y)x gradient plus 2 lam w (lessons 5 and 8), early stopping with patience 5 (lesson 9), then a single test evaluation (lesson 10).
Real output of the two parts run together (NumPy 2.5). Columns: epoch, training loss, validation loss.

blocks.title: Learning curves: cross-entropy per epoch

scenes.caption: Training loss falls fast in the first 10 epochs (0.553 to 0.359), then flattens near 0.338.

Validation loss tracks it a little higher and stops improving: its last gain of more than 0.0001 is 0.3617 at epoch 30. Epoch 35 dips to 0.3616, too small to count, so after five such epochs early stopping fires and restores the epoch-30 weights.

blocks.md: Reading the result. The training and validation curves stay close, so this 3-parameter model is not overfitting; early stopping here simply ends training once it stops paying off. On a high-capacity model the validation curve would turn upward, as in lesson 9, and the same code would catch it. On the 120 test rows (61 positives) the model flags 68, of which 54 are right: precision 54/68 = 0.794 and recall 54/61 = 0.885.

blocks.title: The learned boundary in the original feature units

scenes.caption: Converted back from standardized units, the boundary is x2 = -49.3 x1 + 64.9: a line that separates the two cloud centers.
Points above and to the right get p > 0.5. Raising the threshold would slide this line toward the class 1 center, trading recall for precision (lesson 10).

blocks.prompt: Delete the standardization (use the raw features) and run the same code with learning rate 0.1. What do you expect?
blocks.reveal: Training breaks. The second feature's scale of about 40 makes its curvature roughly 1,600 times larger (40 squared, lesson 3), so a step of 0.1 is far above the stability limit along it. In our run the training loss jumps to 6.2 at epoch 0 and then swings between about 2.7 and 10.4 from epoch to epoch (the printed epochs 5, 10 and 15 show 7.4, 7.1 and 7.5), early stopping fires at epoch 17 on noise, and test precision falls to 0.64.

blocks.md: A complete training loop is: split, fit preprocessing on train, shuffle each epoch, step on minibatch gradients plus the penalty gradient, watch validation loss, keep the best weights, and evaluate on test once. Every bug in later, bigger models is a violation of one of these steps.

blocks.question: Someone runs this code with lam = 1.0 instead of 0.001. Validation loss stalls at about 0.63 and the weights end near (0.13, 0.13). What happened?
options: The penalty dominates the loss, shrinking the weights so much that predictions stay near 0.5: underfitting
The model overfits because lambda is large
Early stopping fired too late
The data were not shuffled
blocks.explain: With $\lambda = 1$ the term $\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$ outweighs the gain from fitting, so the weights stay tiny, every $p$ stays near 0.5, and the loss stays close to $\ln 2 = 0.693$. Strong regularization trades variance for bias, and here bias wins. Choose $\lambda$ on validation data.

blocks.question: A teammate deletes the line w, b = keep, so the test evaluation uses the weights from epoch 35 instead of the saved epoch-30 copy. What changes in this run, and when would it matter?
options: Almost nothing here, since validation loss barely moved after epoch 30; on a model whose validation loss turns upward, it would test the overfit weights early stopping was meant to avoid
The test precision becomes undefined
Training would never stop
Standardization would start using test statistics
blocks.explain: Early stopping has two halves: stop, and return the best saved copy. Here epochs 30 to 35 differ by under 0.0001 in validation loss, so the weights are nearly the same. On a high-capacity model the last patience epochs are exactly the ones where validation loss rose (lesson 9), so skipping the restore keeps the worse weights.

blocks.question: A teammate computes mu and sd on all 600 rows instead of the training rows. The test precision barely changes. Why is it still a bug?
options: It is not a bug, since the effect is small
It makes training slower
It changes the decision threshold
Test rows influenced the model, so the test score is no longer a clean estimate; on other data or steps the leak can be large
blocks.explain: Preprocessing fit on held-out rows is leakage (lesson 11). For a mean and standard deviation on 600 similar rows the effect happens to be small, but the test score is no longer computed on data the pipeline never saw, and the same habit with feature selection inflated accuracy from 0.48 to 0.87.
